newsitem.title: UK: Losses lurk below investment banking profits gloss.
newsitem.headline: Losses lurk below investment banking profits gloss.

text.p: Investment banking can be highly profitable in the good times, but despite industry attempts to tighten controls, the scope for spectacular losses has not diminished.

Britain's National Westminster Bank Plc is the latest in a long casualty list with the revelation that it has had to write off 77 million pounds ($123 million) as a result of mispricing in its interest rate options book over more than two years.

What has surprised many in the banking world is that NatWest's losses and a 180 million pound "black hole" in funds detected last year at Morgan Grenfell Asset Management (MGAM) have occurred in the aftermath of the collapse of British merchant bank Barings in 1995.

Barings met its end as a result of unauthorised derivatives trades totalling $1.4 billion run up by Singapore-based trader Nick Leeson. Leeson is currently serving a jail sentence in Singapore after being convicted on forgery and fraud charges.

Barings was bailed-out by Dutch financial services giant Internationale Nederlanden Groep NV but the shockwaves of the blue-blooded bank's demise were felt throughout the banking world as firms scrambled to make sure such a nightmare scenario could never happen to them.
Regulators around the world have worked to put in place rules and guidelines which they hope will make firms more vigilant when assessing their risk profiles and the competence of their staff.
"You have to ask why things went wrong at NatWest. Who knows whether it was a matter of general mistakes? But clearly heads have rolled," one regulatory source told Reuters.

NatWest on Thursday announced the suspension of four senior employees but stressed this was normal procedure and did not suggest they were responsible for systematic mispricing of interest rate options.

The Securities and Futures Authority (SFA), Britain's financial watchdog, is looking into the conduct of all four, as well as the role of NatWest Market's global head of options and an options trader who left the firm last year.

Options are contracts which give buyers the right, but not the obligation, to buy or sell an underlying security at a set price on a set date in the future. NatWest is investigating how in this case the options traded had been priced wrongly over a long period.
The seriousness with which banks treated the Barings debacle was underlined in the wake of the affair by NatWest chairman Lord Alexander who said in April 1995 that NatWest sought to minimise risk.

At the time he said NatWest maintained clear policies on derivatives, including the setting of "prudent risk limits", establishing clear reporting lines, separating the front and back offices, intensive training for all staff working in derivatives and strict control procedures.
NatWest's losses come at a time when the SFA is about to publish details of an initiative to make senior executives bear greater responsibility in the event of a major management failure.

But whatever safety-nets are put in place to prevent losses being covered up or getting out of control, traders say that if they make a big loss that could cost them their job, they may as well try and trade their way out of it, even if this risks a bigger loss developing.
"If you are in trouble, you are really in trouble and you'll do anything to get out of it," an options trader on the floor of LIFFE, London's main derivatives exchange, told Reuters.

Concern over spiralling performance-related bonuses, increasingly used to motivate traders and others in the investment banking world, has also been voiced by the Bank of England and key industry figures.
While no one has so far lost their job at NatWest as a result of the affair, the bank said it had cut eight million pounds of bonuses to certain individuals in its global debt derivatives division.
And NatWest Market's chief executive Martin Owen has forgone 200,000 of his 500,000 pound bonus for 1996. ($ = 0.626 British Pounds)
